data.text/markdown:
Combining Tables with JOIN

In this notebook we put tables back together to answer questions that no single table can answer. We start with the towns and their counties, then move to the Northwind orders, their lines, their products and their categories. Along the way we count the rows before and after each join, and we find the rows a join leaves out. After class, you will ask the same kind of question of a database on a server.
✏️ Your turn. Add cells with the + button
🚀 This week's work
For a written answer, add a cell under the question, open the cell's ⋯ menu and choose Convert to Markdown. Every ✏️ is part of this week's work. The Going further at the end of an exercise is optional; try it once the rest is done.

Work with your agent the same way as in notebook 6. Try it yourself first, or write the steps in words. Then ask your agent, ask it to explain any line you could not have written, and ask which concepts its answer used. Do exercise A by hand.

The data. This notebook uses two ready-made databases from the course website. combining-towns.duckdb holds the same towns and counties as notebook 6, and combining-northwind.duckdb holds the Northwind tables, the warehouse the SQL handbook uses. The tables have no keys. The next cell downloads both files into your data folder the first time you run it.

What is in the database. Before we write a query, it is a good idea to ask the database which tables and columns it has, because an ERD drawn somewhere else can use other names. Both databases you query in this notebook, DuckDB here and SQL Server in section 5, keep that list in information_schema, a set of tables we can read with SELECT. The following query lists the tables in the Northwind database.

1. Putting Tables Back Together

The towns table keeps only the name of each town's county. To see a town beside its county's population, we have to combine towns with counties. JOIN names the second table, and ON specifies which rows go together, here a town and the county it names. The following query lists the five largest towns with the population of their counties.

✏️ A · Towns and Their Counties

No agent for this one, and no code completion either. When the editor suggests code in grey as you type, press Esc and keep typing your own.
  1. Copy the first query of this section into a cell of your own, remove its LIMIT, and count the rows it returns. In a markdown cell under it, explain why the count is the same as the number of rows in towns. Check yourself: 351.
  2. Add a column with each town's share of its county's population, in percent and rounded to one decimal place, and list the five largest shares. Check yourself: Nantucket 100.0, Boston 84.9, Pittsfield 33.5, Springfield 33.4, Oak Bluffs 25.7.
  3. In the same markdown cell, explain why Nantucket's share is exactly 100.
Going further. For each county, find the town with the largest share of its people.

2. What a Join Leaves Out

JOIN keeps only the rows that have a match in the other table. If a county has no matching town, that county is not in the result, and there is no error message or warning. To find those counties, we can use LEFT JOIN, which keeps every row of the table on the left, here counties. If a county has no matching town, the columns from towns contain NULL in that row, and WHERE t.name IS NULL keeps exactly those rows. The following query finds the counties with no town whose average bill is over $15,000.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='DnEU-0' random-id='f26aa5d0-b041-307e-1226-288bbc3ed19d'><marimo-table data-initial-value='[]' data-label='null' data-data='"[{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Weston\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":26313},{\"name\":\"Norfolk\",\"name_1\":\"Brookline\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":26237},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Lincoln\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":20780},{\"name\":\"Norfolk\",\"name_1\":\"Wellesley\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":20551},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Concord\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":20517},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Lexington\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":20394},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Sherborn\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":20018},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Belmont\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":19579},{\"name\":\"Norfolk\",\"name_1\":\"Dover\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":19088},{\"name\":\"Middlesex\",\"name_1\":\"Winchester\",\"average_single_family_bill_dollars\":18272}]"' data-total-rows='31' data-total-columns='3' data-max-columns='50' data-banner-text='""' data-pagination='true' data-page-size='10' data-field-types='[["name",["string","str"]],["name_1",["string","str"]],["average_single_family_bill_dollars",["integer","i64"]]]' data-show-filters='true' data-show-download='true' data-show-search='true' data-show-column-summaries='true' data-show-data-types='true' data-show-page-size-selector='true' data-show-column-explorer='true' data-show-chart-builder='true' data-row-headers='[]' data-hidden-columns='[]' data-has-stable-row-id='false' data-lazy='false' data-preload='false'></marimo-table></marimo-ui-element>

data.text/markdown:
The result has 10 of the 14 counties. Each of the other four has at least one town with a bill over $15,000. The bill condition is in ON, which decides what counts as a match. If we move it to WHERE, the query runs without an error, but the result is empty. WHERE keeps rows after the join, and for a county with no such town the bill is NULL, which is not over $15,000. A query like this one, which finds the rows in one table that have no match in another, is called an anti join. When you write a JOIN, it is a good idea to check which rows it left out, and an anti join is one way to do that. RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the table on the right, and FULL JOIN keeps every row of both tables. For towns and counties, JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and FULL JOIN all return the same 351 rows, because every town names a county in counties and every county has towns. With a few shows from the TV show database, each join returns a different number of rows. On TV shows:
  • The four shows, with LEFT JOIN
  • The four shows, with RIGHT JOIN
  • The four shows, with FULL JOIN
  • The Office shows with no rating
  • ON and WHERE

✏️ B · The Territories Nobody Covers

In Northwind, employee_territories pairs each employee with the territories they cover. Find the territories in territories that nobody covers, using LEFT JOIN and IS NULL. Check yourself: four territories, Columbia, Bentonville, Dallas and Austin. Going further. List the employees with the number of territories each covers, and check that the counts add up to the rows of employee_territories. Then find the same four territories with WHERE NOT EXISTS (...).

3. When a Join Repeats Rows

In Northwind, an order can have many lines, and each line is a row in order_details. When we join orders to order_details, the result has one row for each line. An order with three lines appears three times, and its Freight value is repeated in each of those rows. To see the effect, we can count the rows in orders, in order_details, and in the result of the join.

Compute the total freight for each ShipCountry, with the largest first, counting each order's freight once. 4. A Chain of Joins

A line in order_details has a ProductID, and a product in products has a CategoryID. So to compute revenue by category, we need three tables: order_details, products and categories. Each JOIN adds one table, with its own ON. On TV shows: A chain of joins

✏️ D · Revenue by Category

A line's revenue is UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount). Compute the total revenue for each category, for the orders shipped to the USA, with the largest first. ShipCountry is in orders, so this query needs a fourth table. Then check that the categories add up to the USA's revenue computed from orders and order_details alone. Check yourself: Beverages first, with about 13,375,939, and all eight, added before rounding, give 63,856,337.63. Going further. Compute revenue by category for each year, and find the category that grew the most.

5. After Class: The Same Joins on a Server

So far every database we have used is a file on your computer. Most companies keep theirs on a server, and you connect to it over the network. Babson runs one with AdventureWorks, a bicycle company's sales database, on Microsoft SQL Server. The version of SQL that SQL Server uses is called T-SQL. It differs from DuckDB's in small ways: tables are inside schemas, as in Sales.SalesOrderHeader, and you write TOP 5 after SELECT where DuckDB writes LIMIT 5 at the end. Set it up once:
  1. In a Terminal in the root folder of your repository, run uv add "pymssql==2.4.5" python-dotenv. Keep the version number: this one also installs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14, where the newest does not. If the install fails on an older Mac, email me.
  2. Open .gitignore in the root folder and check that it lists .env. If it does not, add the line .env and commit that first. Your repository is public, and a password committed once stays in its history. The cell below does not connect until .gitignore lists .env.
  3. Make a file named exactly .env in the root folder, in VS Code. Copy into it the four lines on the Connecting to SQL Server page, in the Class Information module on Canvas. If you change .env later, run your query cell again: marimo does not notice a change to a file on its own.
  4. Before every commit, look at the list of changed files in GitHub Desktop. If .env is in the list, it is not ignored: do not commit.
The cell below reads the server, the login and the password from .env, so they never appear in the notebook. It defines ask_server, which works like ask but takes only the query.
If the connection works, the cell shows the first five orders in Sales.SalesOrderHeader.

6. Practice for the Database Project

The questions in Part B of the database project use a few patterns that the sections above do not show on their own. The exercises below practice them on Northwind, and each one names the project questions that are like it.

✏️ F · Every Territory With Its Count

For each territory, count the employees who cover it, and keep the territories that nobody covers in the result, with 0. A common error is to count with count(*). After a LEFT JOIN, a territory with no match still has one row, so count(*) gives it 1. Count a column from employee_territories instead, because count skips NULL. Check yourself: 53 rows. Four of them have 0, and the counts add up to 49, the number of rows in employee_territories. In the project: like scenario B's question 2 and scenario D's question 4. Going further. For each region, the number of territories and the number of them that somebody covers.

✏️ G · Orders and Territories for Each Employee

Build one row per employee with their number of orders and their number of territories. Then check each count against counting it on its own, from orders alone and from employee_territories alone. Check yourself: Robert has 1,789 orders and 10 territories. If you join both tables to employees in one query and count the rows, Robert gets 17,890, one row for each pair of an order and a territory. In the project: like scenario A's question 6 and scenario D's question 6, and the note under scenario C's questions. Going further. Add each employee's total freight, and check it against orders alone.

✏️ H · The Last 90 Days

The last order in Northwind was placed on 2023-10-28. For each shipper, compute the number of orders and the total freight in the 90 days before that date, with the most orders first. In orders, the shipper is ShipVia, which holds a ShipperID. To keep the orders of those 90 days, use WHERE OrderDate >= DATE '2023-10-28' - INTERVAL 90 DAY. Chapter B, §12 of the SQL handbook has more on dates. Check yourself: 328 orders in all, and United Package first, with 115 orders and 31,827.75 in freight. In the project: like scenario A's question 4, scenario B's question 1 and scenario C's question 7. Going further. The number of orders for each shipper in each month of 2023.

✏️ I · Categories Above the Average

Compute the revenue of each category, then keep only the categories whose revenue is above the average of all the category totals. This needs a query inside another query, called a subquery, which chapter C, §21 of the SQL handbook explains. Check yourself: four categories, Beverages, Confections, Meat/Poultry and Dairy Products. The average is about 56,048,329. In the project: like scenario A's question 4 and scenario C's question 3. Going further. The products whose revenue is above the average of their own category.
